It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 14:00 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T21:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 63.367 degrees and its azimuth is 206.962 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 50.94 degrees and its azimuth is 157.604 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.95 percent illuminated, 28.172 degrees from the Sun, and 371351.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with the naked eye right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Solar Glare)
The most significant factor is the Sun's position. You mentioned the Sun is at an altitude of **63.367 degrees**. This means the Sun is very high in the sky, creating intense, direct daylight. Even though the Moon is also above the horizon, the sheer amount of scattered sunlight in the atmosphere (Rayleigh scattering) creates a "washout" effect. The blue of the sky is so saturated that the faint crescent of a 5.95% illuminated Moon would be completely drowned out.

### 2. The Moon's Phase and Proximity
At only **5.95% illumination**, the Moon is a very thin crescent. While a full moon is easy to see during the day, a thin crescent is much harder because it lacks surface area to reflect light. Furthermore, it is only **28.172 degrees** away from the Sun. Because it is so close to the Sun in the sky, it is sitting in the brightest part of the solar glare.

### 3. Contrast
For an object to be visible to the human eye during the day, it generally needs to have high contrast against the background. Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in this scenario, the "background" (the sky) is at its brightest possible point. The contrast between the tiny sliver of the Moon and the brilliant daylight sky is insufficient for the human eye to distinguish it.

### Summary
While your app confirms the Moon is technically "above the horizon," it is effectively "hidden" by the brilliance of the day. Unless you were looking through high-powered binoculars or a telescope (which would help block out some of the ambient sky light), **you would not be able to spot it.**

You can relax—the Moon is there, but it is invisible to you!
